title: Chrome profile identity and shared credentials: spec
desc: Why saved passwords and cookies vanish: the Chrome user-data-dir is named after the CDP port, a volatile value, so a port change silently creates an empty profile. Spec of the constraint, the options and the recommended order.
steps: PROBLEM: saved passwords and cookies vanish frequently because the Chrome user-data-dir is NAMED AFTER THE PORT, and the port is volatile. WHEN: designing or debugging Chrome profile persistence, or investigating why a login had to be redone. HOW: run wkappbot skill read cdp-open-reuse-existing-chrome-tab for the reuse-probe that depends on this layout, then read csharp/src/WKAppBot.WebBot/ChromeLauncher.LaunchArgs.cs line 14 for the launch string and ChromeLauncher.ProcessDiscovery.cs line 45 for the path convention. WHY, measured 2026-08-27: the launch passes --user-data-dir pointing at chrome-profiles/cdp{port}/, and the port is SHA256-derived per working directory. TWO CONSEQUENCES FOLLOW and the second is the one that actually hurts. A different repo means a different port means a different profile, so credentials never carry across repos -- that half is intentional isolation. But the SAME repo also loses everything the moment its port changes for any reason, because the profile NAME contains the port, so a reassignment silently creates a brand-new empty profile instead of reopening the old one. Profile identity is bound to a VOLATILE resource rather than a stable one. Corroborating evidence in the same file: PrepareLaunchProfile still carries migration code for TWO earlier layouts, chrome-profile and then chrome-profiles/{ProjectHash}, each of which stranded profiles when the convention moved.

DECISION: THE OWNER DESIGN, stated 2026-08-27 in two parts, and it resolves the constraint rather than colliding with it. PART ONE: both appbot and the human use Chrome's DEFAULT user-data-dir, the real profile, so credentials are not synced, copied or isolated -- they are simply the user's own and there is nothing left to lose. PART TWO: repo separation stops living in the profile folder and moves to the PROCESS START FOLDER, which appbot leaves as a hint so each repo can still be told apart. WHEN: implementing shared credentials, or reviewing why the per-project profile folder is being retired. HOW: run wkappbot skill read exec-console-binding-constitution before touching this, because part two brushes against Article 1, then read csharp/src/WKAppBot.WebBot/ChromeLauncher.PortRegistry.cs which ALREADY implements the mechanism this design needs. WHY THE ARTICLE-1 TENSION IS REAL AND ALSO ALREADY SOLVED: Article 1 says the console is the identity and the working folder is NOT, forbidding selection of a partner process by working directory, because on this machine every AI session shares the same repo root as its CWD so a CWD match selects a stranger with high probability. Article 9 draws the line that saves this design: that prohibition governs BINDING, meaning driving input into a console, while ADOPTION -- claiming a long-lived process that shares no console with the caller -- is a different act on a different path, and for adoption the repo genuinely IS the identity. Article 9's condition is the whole of it: the claim must be PUBLISHED, not guessed. So the rule here is exact. A launch that REGISTERS pid, port and repo root at startup and is later found by READING that registry is Article 9 adoption and is correct. A lookup that ENUMERATES running Chromes and picks whichever CWD matches is the Article 1 CWD-selector and is forbidden, however alike the two look from outside. AND THE REGISTRY ALREADY EXISTS: PortRegistry persists the launched port to a runtime file keyed by project hash, which is precisely the published claim, so this is wiring an existing capability rather than building one.

TODO: THE ONE THING THE OWNER DESIGN STILL HAS TO ANSWER -- with a shared default profile there can be only ONE Chrome process and therefore only ONE debugging port, so per-repo PORTS cannot survive and separation has to become per-TAB. WHEN: implementing the shared-default-profile design, and before touching the CDP port discipline rules. HOW: run wkappbot skill read cdp-open-reuse-existing-chrome-tab for the reuse path and wkappbot skill read cdp-command-guide for the port model, then decide the registry's KEY -- it maps repo to PORT today, and under this design it must map repo to TARGET, meaning the tab or window that repo owns inside the one browser. WHY: Chrome runs one process per user-data-dir, so the moment the profile is shared the port stops being a per-repo resource. The process start folder can still say which repo LAUNCHED a Chrome, but it cannot hand two repos separate ports out of one process. TWO STANDING RULES CHANGE AS A RESULT, and neither should move quietly. The global CDP port discipline currently makes a per-project port MANDATORY and forbids connecting to the user's personal Chrome outright -- under this design appbot IS in the user's personal Chrome by intent, so that rule needs rewriting rather than quiet violation. And the taskkill classifier currently PROTECTS the user's personal Chrome by treating a different parent tree as the user's; once appbot shares that process, protected and controlled become the same object, which needs a decision rather than a discovery. THE SECURITY TRADE, stated once so it is a choice and not a surprise: a debugging port opened on the REAL profile means any local process can drive a fully logged-in browser, so the port binding and its lifetime stop being a convenience detail and become the security boundary of the entire design.

INCIDENT: THIS DIAGNOSIS IS A REDISCOVERY, and that fact is itself worth more than the diagnosis. WHEN: opening this spec, before treating any part of it as new ground. HOW: run wkappbot skill read jobkorea-naver-login-wipe-tracker-ref FIRST -- its step 3 already recorded the port-profile mismatch on 2026-06-05, naming three live CDP ports each holding a separate profile and describing the exact symptom, that a login made under one port profile is absent when a later cdp open selects a different one. WHY THE REDISCOVERY MATTERS: on 2026-08-27 this was re-derived from source without that record ever surfacing. A wkhippo recall on chrome user-data-dir shared profile cookies lost returned 91 matches and not one of them was this tracker -- it matched session-closing boilerplate instead. A skill search for chrome profile user-data-dir cookies DID surface it, ranked below the freshly-written spec. So the tracker was reachable by SKILL SEARCH and not by RECALL, which is a retrieval gap worth knowing before you trust an empty recall as evidence that a subject is untouched. WHAT THE NEW READING GENUINELY ADDS, and it is the link between that tracker's step 3 and its step 4: the user-data-dir is literally NAMED chrome-profiles/cdp{port}, so a broken port detection does not merely select a different port -- it selects a different FOLDER, and the profile is gone by construction rather than by accident. That is also why the SAME repo loses credentials and not only a different one, which the 2026-06-05 record did not explain. Cross: jobkorea-naver-login-wipe-tracker-ref, jobkorea-naver-login-wipe-tracker.

CORRECTION 2026-08-29: PART ONE OF THE OWNER DESIGN IS NOT IMPLEMENTABLE ON A CURRENT CHROME, and this must be read before anyone starts building it. WHEN: about to implement the shared-default-profile half of step 2, or about to treat step 3's registry question as the first obstacle -- it is not, this is. HOW: check the installed Chrome major version before designing anything (the version is the directory name under Program Files/Google/Chrome/Application; do NOT run chrome.exe --version on Windows, it does not print to stdout, it LAUNCHES a browser -- measured, it opened a Chrome and timed out the shell). If the major is 136 or later, the shared-default-profile route is closed and the design decision is the one below instead. WHY: from Chrome 136 onward --remote-debugging-port and --remote-debugging-pipe are IGNORED when the target is the default user data directory; they are only honoured together with a --user-data-dir pointing at a NON-standard directory. The stated motivation is exactly our use case seen from the other side -- after App-Bound Encryption shipped, attackers moved to Chrome remote debugging to extract cookies, and a non-default data directory uses a different encryption key, so the restriction is what keeps profile data protected. Source: developer.chrome.com/blog/remote-debugging-port. This machine measured 151.0.7922.175 on 2026-08-29, so the block is live here and now, not a future concern. CONSEQUENCE, and it re-frames the whole spec: 'share the real profile' cannot mean 'share the default user-data-dir'. The owner's INTENT still stands and is reachable two ways, and the choice between them is the actual decision. (1) NARROW, and it fixes the reported pain today: keep a non-default user-data-dir but make its NAME STABLE instead of port-derived, so a port reassignment stops silently creating an empty folder. Ports stay per-repo, the CDP port discipline and the taskkill classifier are untouched, and step 3's registry question never fires. (2) WIDE: one appbot-owned profile shared across repos, which does collapse to a single Chrome process and a single port, so step 3's repo-to-TARGET registry migration becomes required and both standing rules need rewriting -- and credential sharing with the human is then achieved by signing in ONCE inside that profile with Chrome Sync, never by pointing at the default directory. A WARNING BEFORE PICKING (1): PrepareLaunchProfile still carries migration code for a chrome-profiles/{ProjectHash} layout, which means a stable per-repo key was already tried and abandoned once. Find out WHY it was abandoned before re-adopting it, or you will walk back into whatever ended it.

RESOLVED 2026-08-29: WHY THE STABLE {ProjectHash} PROFILE LAYOUT WAS ABANDONED -- and why that reason NO LONGER HOLDS, which is what unblocks the narrow fix. WHEN: about to restore a stable per-repo profile folder name, or weighing whether re-adopting the pre-2026-05-07 layout walks back into a known problem. HOW: the answer is in commit 90fb16f5e55e49cf544612293cf560407beab2cf, 2026-05-07 17:30, titled 'feat(chrome-profile): rename profile dirs to cdp={port}/ + launcher auto-routes to .new.exe'. Read it with git show; do not re-derive this. WHAT IT SAYS, quoted: 'Profile name embeds the CDP port number so the owning Chrome is unambiguous at a glance (WMI cmdline, directory listing, log messages)', and from the diff comments, 'With the new naming the port is literally embedded in the profile dir name -- no separate registry needed' and 'FAST PATH: when the udd uses the new cdp{port}/ layout, the port is literally embedded in the directory name. No WMI scan needed -- regex-extract the trailing cdp=(d+)'. So the folder name was never merely a name: it is a PORT-DISCOVERY CHANNEL, read back by ProcessDiscovery.cs:45 out of a running Chrome's --user-data-dir argument. The stable hash layout was abandoned because it could not serve that channel, and it had lived only SIX DAYS, 2026-05-01 to 2026-05-07. THE REASON IS NOW OBSOLETE, and this is the whole point: the registry the commit set out to avoid WAS SUBSEQUENTLY BUILT -- ChromeLauncher.PortRegistry.cs exposes RegisterLaunchedPort(int), GetLaunchedPort() and UnregisterPort(), a published claim keyed by project hash. The justification for embedding the port in the path therefore no longer stands; what remains is only the cost, which the owner has now stated in his own words: the port-keyed layout is inconvenient and cookies and passwords are wiped constantly. SO THE FIX SHAPE IS SETTLED: restore a STABLE folder key, and resolve the port from the registry instead of parsing it out of the path. Anything that today regex-extracts cdp=(d+) from a user-data-dir must be repointed at GetLaunchedPort first, with the path parse kept only as a legacy fallback for profiles that still carry the old name. ONE MORE FINDING FROM THE SAME DAY, and it bears directly on the owner's ownership directive: commit 4d2b6ccc7d, 2026-05-07 20:54, fixed CROSS-PROJECT CHROME THEFT introduced by the port-based layout -- projects sharing one wkappbot.exe binary could claim each other's Chrome. Ownership enforcement in this tree is therefore already real and already keyed to the PORT: a Global wkappbot-chrome-profile-{port} named mutex at ChromeLauncher.LaunchCore.cs:22 taken BEFORE any reuse, and IsOwnPort at WebCommands.Part3.EnsureChrome.cs:102-117 which states in its own comment that there are two ways a port can be ours and BOTH are needed, refusing to launch on a port neither claims. What the owner asked for on 2026-08-29 is a change of KEY, not a new mechanism: bind ownership to the CALLER WINDOW that launched the Chrome rather than to the port, which is reachable because the caller hwnd already crosses the pipe as the __hwnd prefix -- record it in the claim at registration and compare it on access. HONEST LIMIT: a delegated history dig reported this as 'reason not recorded' because the commit states the new layout's BENEFIT rather than the old one's fault. That reading is too strict -- a benefit that the design was rebuilt to obtain IS the reason -- but the distinction is worth keeping, because it means no defect of the hash layout was ever documented, and none was found in six days of use.

SETTLED 2026-08-31: BOTH GetDefaultUserDataDir overloads now return GetSharedUserDataDir() unconditionally. The no-arg overload previously returned the shared appbot profile only when ProjectHash was set and fell back to GetMasterUserDataDir() otherwise -- so which profile a caller got depended on whether ProjectHash happened to be set at that moment, not on any decision. Both chrome-profiles/appbot and chrome-profiles/master were found live on disk that day beside port-named cdp={port} remnants, which is the physical evidence: a login made under one profile is simply ABSENT when the other is opened, and that is the four-month 'cookies and passwords keep getting wiped' report -- nothing was ever wiped, a different folder was opened. TWO THINGS THE FIX DOES NOT DO. (1) It does not migrate the existing master profile; those credentials stay stranded until someone moves them deliberately. (2) GetMasterUserDataDir() still exists and is still callable -- the split cannot be called closed until its remaining call sites are audited. VERIFY BY LAUNCHING THE SAME REPO TWICE AND CONFIRMING ONE FOLDER, never by reading the resolver: this defect's whole nature was that both branches looked correct in isolation.

RESULT 2026-09-05: the ownership LOOKUP is now wired on the launch path, closing the recording-without-reading gap this spec's step 4 left open. WHEN: you are tracing why a tab opened in another working folder's browser window, or about to add a seam to the launch path. HOW: run wkappbot skill read cdp-tab-sovereignty-no-cross-agent-interference for the charter, then read TryReuseExistingChromeAsync in ChromeLauncher.LaunchPreparation.cs -- it now calls FindChromeOwnedByCallerAsync with the caller hwnd, reads the port property off the owned window, and reuses that port when it is active, falling through to the any-running-Chrome scan otherwise, with a stderr line naming which branch was taken. WHY, AND THE PART THAT COST A ROUND: the obvious seam is ResolveLaunchPortAsync, and it is UNREACHABLE. That function zeroes its resolved port only when the incoming port equals the retired default 9222, and every caller now passes a concrete live port, so the resolved port is non-zero on entry and every block below is skipped. A seam added there is dead code that reviews perfectly. The reachable fall-through is in TryReuseExistingChromeAsync, and a delegate found this by tracing execution rather than by reading the diff -- prove any launch-path change by REACHABILITY first. THE MISS MUST FALL THROUGH AND NEVER REFUSE: refusing here locks the owner out of his own running browser, which is why the separate refusal, IsWindowOwnedBy, stays deliberately unwired until the lookup is proven to answer.

BUG: the ownership ledger OUTLIVES the browser while CDP windowIds are RECYCLED, so a stale row silently grants ownership of a window that is not yours. WHEN: any reasoning about who owns a Chrome window after a browser restart, a crash, a taskkill, or an overnight gap -- and before believing any ownership falsifier that ran on a fresh ledger. HOW: run wkappbot skill read standard-chrome-window for the two gates and the two-caller falsifier, then run that falsifier a SECOND time on a DIRTY bed: kill every Chrome, leave the ledger file in place, and repeat the four opens. The fix is to make the ledger's lifetime match the browser instance -- stamp the browser identity beside each row and treat a row from a different instance as absent, or clear the ledger at launch. Do NOT try to fix it by validating the window at read time: a recycled id IS a valid window, just not yours. WHY: measured 2026-09-06 on staging v7.9.208, minutes after a clean-bed falsifier passed 4/4. With every Chrome force-killed and the ledger untouched, caller 0x180276 printed Opened new tab instead of New window created, and caller 0x1A20710 printed Reusing existing tab E05510C7 -- a targetId belonging to an EARLIER session's window. Separation was broken by nothing but leftover rows. CallerOwnsAnyWindow checks only the caller column and never asks whether the window still exists, and IsWindowOwnedBy matches a recycled windowId just as happily. THE GENERAL LESSON: a falsifier on a clean bed proves the MECHANISM and says nothing about the LIFETIME. Always run the dirty-bed case -- kill the thing, leave the state, try again.

RETRACTED: the stale-ledger finding in the step above is NOT ESTABLISHED -- I withdraw it the same day I wrote it, because the precondition never held. WHEN: before acting on that step, and any time a measurement depends on having killed a process. HOW: run wkappbot skill read taskkill-compat-shim-a11y-first-kill-routing for the kill-routing policy, then NEVER trust a kill report -- prove the kill with an independent liveness check and compare START TIMES, not just counts, so a respawn cannot masquerade as a survivor. The check that settles it is a PowerShell Get-Process on the image name printing the count, and it must read zero before any conclusion is drawn. WHY: measured 2026-09-06. wkappbot taskkill --force printed Killed: 9 / Preserved: 11 on three separate invocations while killing NOTHING -- immediately afterwards Get-Process chrome reported nine alive, and they were the SAME pids with their ORIGINAL StartTime values, so they had neither died nor restarted. Its own stderr shows the a11y layer SKIPping each pid as a foreign family tree and the summary counting those skips as KILLED. Chrome therefore never restarted during my test, CDP windowIds were never recycled, and the Opened new tab and Reusing existing tab results I recorded as a bug were CORRECT behaviour on live windows. THE LESSON THAT SURVIVES IS THE ONE I FAILED TWICE: a falsifier is only as good as its PRECONDITION, and a tool that reports success is not evidence the state changed. The clear-on-launch code that shipped for this is defensible on its own terms but was NOT justified by a proven defect, and must not be cited as one.

RESULT 2026-09-07: the reachable ownership seam this skill step 5 records now speaks on its THIRD outcome, and the letters that called it untouched were stale. WHAT WAS MEASURED, by a census sector rather than inferred: line 193 of ChromeLauncher.LaunchPreparation.cs sits inside TryReuseExistingChromeAsync declared at line 181, and LaunchCore.cs calls that method at lines 42 and 86, so the consult is wired and reachable. Three successive predecessor letters listed it as untouched; it was not. WHAT CHANGED: the method had three outcomes and only two of them spoke. The success branch prints which window and port it reused. An honest miss falls through silently and correctly. A THROW anywhere inside the consult was swallowed by a bare catch, so a broken lookup and a caller that owns nothing produced byte-identical logs -- and those two need opposite responses. The catch now names the exception type and message on the reuse phase and still falls through. THE FALL-THROUGH IS UNCHANGED BY DESIGN, per this skill step 5: a miss must NEVER refuse or the owner is locked out of his own running browser. WHAT I NEARLY WROTE INTO THE SOURCE AND DID NOT: my first draft of that comment asserted the consult is INERT because FindChromeOwnedByCallerAsync reads a Win32 window property while ownership is recorded to a windowId-keyed ledger, which is the disjoint-store defect the project CLAUDE.md records for WebCommands.Part3.OwnershipGate.cs. Reading step 5 first showed the inference does not transfer: this site was chosen deliberately as the REACHABLE seam after ResolveLaunchPortAsync was found unreachable. So whether the two ownership stores actually agree HERE is still an open question and must be settled by a run, not by analogy -- the two-caller falsifier in standard-chrome-window is the instrument. THE RULE: an unverified inference in canonical source costs the same as one in a skill, and a comment is read as fact by everyone after you.

requirements.expect: the launch string passes --user-data-dir with the port-named path
